content.title: About
content.content: Beef short ribs are a cut from the cow’s rib cage that includes meat and bone marrow. They are known for a rich, beefy flavor, juiciness, and a distinctive texture thanks to the connective tissue that turns gelatinous when cooked slowly.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Short ribs are a staple in many cuisines, such as American barbecue and Korean galbi.
When braised low and slow, the meat becomes so tender that the bones easily separate.
In the United States you’ll find “baby back ribs” (from the top of the rib cage) and “short ribs” (from the lower rib area), each with different meat‑to‑bone ratios.
The high collagen content breaks down into gelatin during long cooking, giving sauces a silky mouthfeel.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Heme iron from beef is readily absorbed and helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function, wound healing, and DNA synthesis.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Short ribs are a good source of B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Collagen and gelatin
items.content: Slow cooking converts collagen to gelatin, which may benefit joint health and digestion.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Excessive intake can raise cholesterol levels; moderation is recommended.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper cooking may allow Salmonella or E. coli to survive; cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: High purine levels can exacerbate gout in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Short ribs are best cooked low and slow: braise, oven‑roast, or grill at low heat. Marinate in soy sauce, honey, spices, and wine for extra flavor. Serve with roasted vegetables, mashed potatoes, or rice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh short ribs in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the fridge before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Octopus is a marine mollusk belonging to the class Cephalopoda, found in warm seas worldwide. Its meat is tender, mildly sweet, and carries a distinct oceanic flavor. It is used in many cuisines, often sliced into rings, served in sushi, salads, or stewed dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Octopuses have eight arms, each lined with suction cups that allow them to grasp and sense their environment.
They are highly intelligent, capable of solving puzzles, using tools, and remembering maze routes.
Most species can change skin color and texture for camouflage.
Octopuses can regenerate lost arms within a few weeks.
In Japan octopus is a delicacy, while in the Mediterranean it is commonly prepared in stews.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Octopus meat provides about 15 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, making it an excellent protein source.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: It contains very little saturated fat, suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Octopus is rich in iron, zinc, magnesium, and selenium, supporting immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: A modest amount of omega‑3 contributes to heart health and reduces inflammation.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to octopus, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Natural toxins
items.content: Certain wild species (e.g., blue‑ringed octopus) contain toxins, but commercially sold varieties are generally safe.

items.title: Food parasites
items.content: Raw or undercooked seafood can harbor parasites; cooking octopus to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C is recommended.

items.title: High sodium in canned forms
items.content: Canned octopus often contains added salt, which may be unsuitable for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Octopus is commonly boiled, grilled, baked, or steamed. It is sliced into rings for salads, sushi, paella, and risotto. Tenderizing by gently beating the meat before cooking improves texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh octopus should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C and used within 1‑2 days. Frozen octopus retains quality for up to 6 months at –18 °C. Thaw in the fridge and rinse thoroughly before preparation.

rice-brown-with-carrots-no-added-fat.title: Brown Rice with Carrots, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice with carrots, prepared without added fat, is a whole‑grain rice cooked together with grated carrots. The oil‑free preparation preserves the natural flavors and nutrients of both ingredients, resulting in a light, aromatic dish rich in fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, giving it more vitamins and minerals than white rice.
Carrots are high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
The lack of added fat makes the dish low‑calorie while still satisfying hunger thanks to fiber.
Rice with carrots is a traditional side in many Asian cuisines, often served as a simple main or accompaniment.
When stored properly, brown rice can stay fresh for up to 6 months.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, helps regulate blood sugar levels, and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of magnesium and selenium
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function, while selenium provides antioxidant protection.

items.title: Vitamin A from carrots
items.content: Beta‑carotene contributes to eye health, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: No added oil makes the dish suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Brown rice delivers slow‑release energy, beneficial for athletes and active individuals.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Like all rice, brown rice may contain trace amounts of arsenic; rinsing before cooking reduces this.

items.title: Carrot allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to carrots.

items.title: Excess beta‑carotene
items.content: Very large portions of carrots can cause temporary yellowing of the skin (carotenemia).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice as a side with vegetables, fish, or poultry. It works well in salads, soups, or as a base for vegetarian bowls. Add fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or low‑sodium soy sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice should be refrigerated and consumed within 3‑4 days. Reheat to at least 75 °C before eating.
